bib.title: Bootstrap your own latent: A new approach to self-supervised Learning

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Bootstrap Your Own Latent: A New Approach to Self-Supervised Learning. Grill, Strub, Altché, Tallec, Richemond et al. (DeepMind). The file is arXiv:2006.07733v3 (10 Sep 2020). You say it was published at NeurIPS 2020, but the PDF itself does not name a venue.

COVERAGE: I read about 75k of 109,142 chars in full: the main text pp.1–11, Appendices A–C and E–I, and J.3. I skimmed Appendix D (transfer implementation details), the rest of J (JAX pseudo-code) and the references, which I used only to check origins.

CLAIMS
- claim: BYOL needs no negatives. An online network (encoder, projector, predictor) is trained to predict the target network's projection of a second view of the same image. The target has no predictor and receives no gradient (stop-gradient), and its weights are an exponential moving average (EMA) of the online weights, with τ going from 0.996 up to 1 on a cosine schedule. The loss is MSE between the l2-normalised vectors, applied in both directions.
  number: 0.996
  quote: "ξ←τξ + (1−τ )θ" ... "τ starts fromτbase = 0.996 and is increased to one during training"
  where: pp.3–5

- claim: Under ImageNet linear evaluation BYOL beats SimCLR at every architecture size tested.
  number: 74.3 vs 69.3 (ResNet-50); 77.4 vs 74.2 (R50 2×, 94M); 78.6 vs 76.5 (R50 4×, 375M); 79.6 best (ResNet-200 2×, 250M)
  setup: 1000 epochs, batch 4096, 512 TPU v3 cores; standard frozen-feature linear probe. The SimCLR figures are the ones published in [8].
  quote: "SimCLR [8] ResNet- 50 (4×) 375M 76.5 93 .2 / BYOL (ours) ResNet- 50 (4×) 375M 78.6 94.2" ; "BYOL (ours) 74.3 91.6"
  where: p.6, Table 1

- claim: BYOL is much less sensitive to batch size than SimCLR.
  number: BYOL 72.5→71.8 vs SimCLR 67.9→64.3 (batch 4096→256)
  setup: 300-epoch ablations, 3 seeds. Smaller batches use gradient accumulation (the paper's "average gradients over N consecutive steps"), and SimCLR is the authors' own reproduction. Both drop at 64 (59.7 vs 59.2), which the authors blame on BatchNorm.
  quote: "256 71 .8 64 .3±2.1"
  where: p.26, Table 16; p.8, Fig 3a

- claim: Removing colour augmentation, or training on crops only, hurts BYOL far less than SimCLR.
  number: −9.1 vs −22.2 points; crop only 59.4 vs 40.3
  setup: same 300-epoch ablation setup
  quote: "(−9.1 accuracy points for BYOL,−22.2 accuracy points for SimCLR)" ; "BYOL still displays good performance ( 59.4%, i.e.−13.1 points from 72.5% ), while SimCLR loses more than a third of its performance (40.3%"
  where: p.8

- claim: The model collapses at τ=0 and stalls at τ=1, and it collapses without the predictor or without the target network. Removing the predictor gives an unsupervised Mean Teacher, which collapses.
  number: τ=0 → 0.3; τ=1 (constant random target) → 18.8; τ 0.9–0.999 → ≥68.4; without negatives (β=0), dropping the predictor or the target → 0.1–0.3
  quote: "Stop gradient of online† 0 0 .3" ; "Constant random network 1 18 .8±0.7" ; "the representation does collapse when either is removed"
  where: p.9, Table 5; p.10

- claim: The target network can be dropped (hard copy, τ=0) if the predictor is kept near-optimal. Two ways work: a closed-form linear predictor fitted on each batch, or a predictor learning rate higher than the projector's.
  number: 52.5% (closed-form linear predictor); 66.5% (higher predictor learning rate)
  quote: "using an optimal linear predictor (obtained by linear regression on the current batch) ... (52.5% top-1 accuracy), or (ii) increasing the learning rate of the predictor (66.5% top-1)"
  where: p.10; App. I, Tables 21–22

LIMITS: There is no proof of why collapse is avoided. The authors say "this objective admits collapsed solutions ... we empirically show that BYOL does not converge to such solutions". They "hypothesize" that the collapsed equilibria are unstable, and that argument assumes an optimal predictor and drops normalisation and symmetrisation (pp.2–5). They also concede that "BYOL's dynamics still admit undesirable equilibria". BYOL still depends on vision-specific augmentations, and the authors say extending it to other modalities needs new ones (p.10). Batch norm stays in the encoder and is the only place batch size enters; the paper does not test BYOL without batch norm. With no weight decay, both BYOL and SimCLR diverge (p.9). All ablations run 300 epochs, not the full 1000. The batch-size and augmentation comparisons use the authors' SimCLR reproduction (67.9 at 300 epochs).

BUILDS ON: SimCLR (Chen et al., arXiv 2020) for augmentations and the projector. MoCo (He et al., arXiv 2019) for the momentum encoder. Mean Teacher (Tarvainen and Valpola, NeurIPS 2017). EMA target networks from deep RL: DQN (Mnih et al.) and DDPG (Lillicrap et al., arXiv 2015). PBL (Guo et al., ICML). DeepCluster (Caron et al., ECCV 2018). Cross-view prediction (Becker and Hinton, Nature 1992). CPC/InfoNCE (van den Oord et al., arXiv 2018).

CODE: The J.3 loss is the negative cosine similarity between the online "prediction" and `jax.lax.stop_gradient(target_network_out_2[ projection ])`, applied in both directions (p.33).

FIGURES: Figure 2, p.4: "BYOL's architecture ... ξ are an exponential moving average of θ and sg means stop-gradient". It shows the asymmetry (predictor on the online side only, stop-gradient on the target) faster than prose. An alternative is Figure 3 (p.8), the batch-size and augmentation drop curves against SimCLR.

PROBLEMS: Appendix I.2 contains an unfilled placeholder: "we obtain a top-1 accuracy offill ." The main text gives 52.5% for the same experiment. In Table 5b the checkmarks extract ambiguously, so I could not reliably say which collapsed row (0.3, 0.2 or 0.1) means "no predictor" and which means "no target". Table 19 is clearer, e.g. "ξ 0 0.2" (target, no predictor). The PDF contains no embedded instructions.
